newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space officials mull over Mir repairs.
newsitem.headline: Russian space officials mull over Mir repairs.

text.p: Russian space officials are pressing ahead with plans to fix the blighted orbiting station Mir, whose tired Russian-American crew has suffered a jinx-like series of mishaps.

The current crew now seem unlikely to carry out the risky repairs, needed after a collision in orbit on June 25 followed by other troubles, including a computer crash caused by human error last Thursday.

Mission director Vladimir Solovyov said simulated tests on Earth had shown the repairs could not be done without taking special equipment to Mir and made clear he expected them to be made by a crew which is due to arrive on Mir on August 7.

"These instruments can only be delivered by the next space craft and then it will be highly unreasonable to send the weary old crew to do the repairs rather than the fresh new crew," he told reporers at Mission Control near Moscow on Saturday.

He said later in a television interview: "I think it is better for us not to propose to this crew that they go out into open space as there is only a little time until the next expedition and the lads are tired."
Solovyov said a final announcement would be made on Monday and added: "I want to repeat that this programme which we are discussing will be confirmed on Monday."

Mission commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin were initially scheduled to return to Earth on August 26, with British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale returning aboard a U.S. shuttle in September.
Two Russian cosmonauts, Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, are in training outside Moscow at Zvyozdny Gorodok to undertake the repair work.
About half of Mir's power was lost when a collision during a manual docking manoeuvre on June 25 pubctured a module attached to the 11-year-old space station.

Some power has been restored, but dangerous repair work involving entering the airless module is needed If the operation goes wrong, Russian space officials say the crew doing the repairs may have to abandon ship.

Problems have plagued the mission since the collision. An unidentified liquid leaked into space, Tsibliyev suffered a heart problem and one of the crew caused the computer to crash last Thursday by pulling out a wrong cable.
Solovyov, looking tired himself, said there was no question of aborting the mission but he made clear that the crew were weary and under stress.
"They have been through a lot, something which has a serious effect on a person's pyschology," he told Russia's ORT television.

The problems on Mir, which was originally expected to have a usueful lifespan of five years, have raised doubts about its future and that of Russian cooperation in space with the United States and other nations.
Asked if the United States would end its participation in the Mir project, U.S. President Bill Clinton said last Thursday that it was too soon for him to draw a conclusion.
